article.articleHeadline: Herpes Simplex Virus | A 30-year-old woman with cracked mouth corners thought it was due to heat; a deadly virus invaded the brain and claimed her life. Doctors warn of three situations where the virus can easily invade.
article.articleSummary: In Shaanxi, China, a 30-year-old woman with cracked mouth corners—initially blamed on heat—developed herpes simplex encephalitis after the herpes simplex virus invaded her central nervous system. Despite early self-treatment, she suffered fever, weakness, facial numbness, severe brain swelling, and ultimately brain death. Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 establish lifelong latency in nerve ganglia and reactivate when immunity is weakened by stress, illness, sleep deprivation, or cold exposure. CNS invasion leads to rapid, potentially irreversible brain inflammation. Untreated herpes encephalitis carries about a 70% mortality and is a major infectious cause of fatal encephalitis in the United States, accounting for roughly 10–20% of the 20,000 annual encephalitis cases. Most HSV infections are self-limited, but five neurological warning signs of CNS involvement necessitate emergency care; the article cautions against panic while urging vigilance.

article.articleHeadline: During the Fifteenth Five-Year Plan period, a joint prevention and control mechanism for major infectious disease outbreaks will be established.
article.articleSummary: China will establish a joint prevention and control mechanism for major infectious disease outbreaks during the 15th Five-Year Plan. Sun Yang, deputy director of the National Center for Disease Control and Prevention, stated at a State Council Information Office briefing that the plan centers on system, capability, and strategy. System: form province–city–county joint prevention and control mechanisms with routine operation, strengthen top‑down leadership, deepen medical–public health integration, and involve village committees in public health governance. Capability: emphasize science and digital empowerment, build a smart disease-control platform, and develop AI models to enable real-time monitoring of fever clinics, outpatient visits, and medical burden. Strategy: pursue multi-disease prevention and calm-to-acute transition, coordinating monitoring, testing, prevention, and control for respiratory diseases—influenza, COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae—with unified surveillance and testing, plus emergency planning and reserves. Goal: a more resilient, modern public health system safeguarding economic and social development.

article.articleSummary: China is accelerating a nationwide shift to a 'smart' multi-point triggering infectious disease surveillance and early-warning system, aiming by 2030 for a modern health network. In Tianjin, 284 medical institutions are connected, covering 42 legally defined infectious diseases and five syndromic presentations; automated prompts guide tests such as HBV panels, enabling proactive detection. In Shanghai’s Jing’an District, December 2025 saw three pneumonia cases with clustering; no close contact found, investigation completed within 24 hours. Since Oct 2025, Shanghai identified over 220,000 infectious pneumonia cases, about 1,300 high-risk cases cleared in 24 hours. The 2025 revision of the Infectious Disease Prevention and Control Law elevated surveillance to a legal obligation and broadened sensor networks for new and unexplained illnesses.

article.articleHeadline: A woman was hit in the face by a bat, treated as the highest risk for rabies! Doctors explain why.
article.articleSummary: On 2026-09-14 in Zhejiang, a woman walking was struck in the face by a bat; despite no visible wound, she is treated as a Level III (highest risk) rabies exposure per China's Rabies Exposure Prevention and Management Guidelines (2023 edition). Level III exposure includes direct bat contact and requires wound irrigation and disinfection, administration of rabies immunoglobulin (passive) and a full rabies vaccination series. Bats are a key high-risk reservoir for the rabies virus, with near-100% fatality once symptomatic. Immediate management after bat exposure: wash the affected area with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes (alternating), disinfect with povidone-iodine or medical alcohol, then seek prompt medical care and report exposure details (time, place, bat condition) to clinicians. Do not chase bats; seal home entry points and screens to prevent indoor encounters.

article.articleHeadline: Digital systems better Yiwu's control of infectious diseases
article.articleSummary: Yiwu, Zhejiang province, uses a digital infectious-disease reporting system that lets fever clinics report cases to disease-control agencies; positive samples are retested in laboratories. The system replaces manual paperwork and phone calls, increasing speed and reducing errors. Nine secondary- or higher-level hospitals and 14 community health centers are equipped with national early warning software that integrates syndromic data from schools and elderly-care homes for early outbreak detection. As of late July 2026, surveillance identified 344 emerging incidents. Despite higher inbound travel, Yiwu has not seen major local transmission from imported cases for mosquito-borne diseases. All major hospitals can perform nucleic acid testing for dengue and chikungunya; epidemiological investigation data can be transferred with samples to CDCs online. Initial diagnosis at first consultation for mosquito-borne diseases is 97.3% (up 10.52 points YoY), with response teams activated within 30 minutes. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) aims to upgrade monitoring platforms and connectivity.

article.articleHeadline: Persistent fever after travel turns out to be melioidosis.
article.articleSummary: On 2026-09-15, a diabetic man returning from Southeast Asia developed persistent fever up to 40°C, cough, and chest pain. After ineffective pneumonia treatment with IV fluids, he received a lab-confirmed diagnosis of melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) at the First Affiliated Hospital of Hunan University of Chinese Medicine. Melioidosis is a tropical soil-borne infection prevalent in wet soils and rice paddies, contracted via skin contact with contaminated mud or water, inhalation of contaminated aerosols, or ingestion of contaminated water; human-to-human transmission is rare. Incubation is 1–4 weeks, potentially longer. High-risk groups include recent travelers to tropical regions (e.g., Hainan, Southeast Asia, northern Australia) within a month, diabetics (risk ~12×; ~75% of cases), and those with chronic kidney/liver/pulmonary disease or certain occupations. Treatment requires 2–4 weeks of intravenous antibiotics in the acute phase, followed by 3–6 months of oral therapy. Preventive measures include waterproofing, protective footwear, masks, boiled water, and thorough hand hygiene.

article.articleHeadline: Uproar over 'Cepirit' at HYROX Beijing: The danger of fecal contamination at sporting events.
article.articleSummary: HYROX Beijing 2026 sparked online debate after Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk suffered encopresis during the Women's Pro Solo but continued and finished with a time of 1:01:23. Organizers assert clear procedures for biological contamination and medical management, but HYROX Official acknowledged that protocols for elite competition and mass-participation can overlap, causing ambiguity in their application. The arena was sterilized to minimize infection risk to other competitors. Dr. Aru Ariadno, SpPD-KGEH FINASIM, notes that fecal contamination at public venues could theoretically transmit diseases through contact or contaminated surfaces, including influenza, Singapore fever, chickenpox, typhoid fever, hepatitis A, and E. coli infections, especially if hands or equipment are not washed. The episode highlights infectious-disease risks at large sporting events and the need for clear, consistently enforced hygiene measures to protect athletes.

article.articleHeadline: Finger cut by scissors progresses to critical condition; a woman in Wuxi is put on a ventilator due to tetanus.
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-09-15, in Wuxi, Jiangsu Province, a woman developed tetanus after a scissors cut on her left index finger during fieldwork and was diagnosed on admission. Delayed proper wound care and tetanus prevention preceded six days of worsening jaw stiffness and dyspnea, culminating in respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation in the Emergency ICU of Nanjing Medical University Affiliated Wuxi People’s Hospital. She received antibiotics, tetanus antitoxin, tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, tetanus vaccination, and fluid support, with shielding to minimize stimuli. After about one week, spasms subsided, respiration improved, and she could communicate and eat; she was discharged cured. High-risk wounds are deep, dirty, or contaminated with rusted objects or soil/dung; prevention combines passive immunity (immunoglobulin/antitoxin) and active vaccination (tetanus vaccines) within routine immunization. Do not abandon small wounds—seek prompt medical care for debridement and tetanus prophylaxis.

article.articleHeadline: 'Kim Seung-won's lobbying allegations' COVID-19 treatment concealed hamster deaths and was administered to 93 patients.

A 1st‑court ruling found Professor Kang Mo violated pharmaceutical law by directing deletion of the unfavorable hamster data. Separate allegations included a 32 billion won government grant-skimming and 5 billion won stock manipulation. MFDS notes no SUSAR reported, but whether trial participants were adequately informed remains unclear.

article.articleHeadline: Why is the antigen kit positive but ELISA negative? A big discrepancy in dengue reports between Bhagalpur's JLNMCH and private labs - Bhagalpur dengue test discrepancy: private vs JLNMCH reports.
article.articleSummary: As of 14 September 2026, seven dengue patients in Bhagalpur were admitted to JLNMCH after private labs reported dengue-positive results, but subsequent government ELISA tests at the hospital were negative, and all seven were discharged. The discrepancy arises because private labs commonly use antigen rapid card kits and CBC, which can flag dengue if platelet counts fall—even though CBC is not a definitive confirmatory test. Government standards consider ELISA as the most authentic diagnostic method. Experts note delayed hospital presentation: patients often seek private testing after 3–4 days of illness and reach the hospital after 5–7 days, by which time the virus in blood wanes and antibodies rise, yielding negative ELISA results. Symptoms include high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, muscle/joint pain, vomiting, and poor appetite. Clinicians advise early ELISA testing within 2–3 days of symptom onset for timely, accurate diagnosis and treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Head injury or nose surgery can open the door to amoebic brain fever: Symptoms to watch out for
article.articleSummary: As of 14 September 2026, Kerala reports a surge in amoebic brain infections linked to water exposure. Naegleria fowleri causes amoebic meningoencephalitis, which can progress rapidly and be fatal; Acanthamoeba infections are also detected. A joint study by the state health department and ICMR found higher risk among people with head injuries or nasal surgery who contracted infection after contact with ordinary water bodies. Risk factors include washing wounds in water bodies, using water from non-chlorinated wells, and water entering the nose. Kerala’s case fatality rate for amoebic meningoencephalitis is 25.8%. In Malappuram, a youth died last month in Kadampuzha; a child undergoing treatment has Acanthamoeba. Authorities urge avoidance of contaminated water bodies during rains and call for regular pond cleaning and proper well chlorination. Early symptoms include fever, headache, and vomiting, with progression to loss of consciousness, disorientation, seizures, and potential death.

article.articleSummary: On 14 September 2026, in Dehradun, Uttarakhand, Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami directed authorities to bolster preparations for preventing infectious diseases, including swine flu. He ordered regular hospital inspections, assessment of sanitation, and availability of medicines and essential medical supplies, with the health department and district administration coordinating for prevention, treatment, and effective containment, and ongoing surveillance. He also instructed DM-level reviews of hospital status in their districts and to ensure timely monitoring of the situation. The CM emphasized improving arrangements for travel and public-health campaigns, including preparations for the Four Dhams pilgrimage and the Seva Sankalp program (phase three). He further announced that after 15 October he would conduct surprise road inspections to oversee implementation.

article.articleHeadline: In Rohtak, an 8-year-old boy dies of TB; his sister had also died a year earlier.
article.articleSummary: In Rohtak, Haryana, an eight-year-old boy, Nooni, died of tuberculosis at PGIMS Rohtak on September 13 after about two months of treatment in Ward 14. His four-month-old sister had died of TB last Raksha Bandhan. The father, Anil, a painter from Muzaffar­nagar, Uttar Pradesh, and resident of Ekta Colony, says his four other children should be screened for TB. Nooni had become very weak and was unable to walk before his illness; on September 9 he collapsed at home after a burn from a teacup, and was subsequently admitted to PGIMS. Shivaji Colony police lodged a report with the CMO after an autopsy. Doctors caution that untreated TB can infect 10–15 contacts. The state TB elimination program has identified 2,111 high-risk rural/urban wards and reports about 32,419 TB patients.

article.articleHeadline: Gross negligence - Three HIV-positive women gave birth to infected children, and the health department shrugged off responsibility.
article.articleSummary: Three HIV-positive women in Gurugram gave birth to HIV-infected children, highlighting gaps in public health response. Deputy Civil Surgeon Dr. Monica Yadav said antiretroviral therapy lowers, but does not guarantee, transmission; in one case the pregnancy went untested until delivery, revealing maternal infection and both spouses were HIV-positive. A second case at SGT University involved poor adherence to medication, leading to an infected newborn. A third case was diagnosed six months after birth. All three cases are under investigation, with counseling being offered to families. Over five years, Gurugram reported 93 HIV-infected children. The district, with a population over 3.5 million and about 60% migrants, has rising HIV confirmations: 302 (2023-24), 272 (2024-25), 300 (2025-26); eight months into 2026 already 229. Authorities cite migrant influx for the increase and face criticism for negligence.

article.articleHeadline: Anti-rabies drive vaccinates 1,485 stray dogs in Dibrugarh since Aug last year
article.articleSummary: Rabies prevention drive in Dibrugarh, Assam, has vaccinated 1,485 stray dogs since Aug 14, 2025. The latest effort at Assam Medical College and Hospital (AMCH) campus vaccinated 90 dogs, including 20 on Sept 14, after 70 were vaccinated Sept 5–13. Overall totals stand at 1,395 up to Sept 4; 70 from Sept 5–13; and 20 on Sept 14. The campaign is led by Animal Welfare People (AWP) in collaboration with the Dibrugarh Municipal Corporation and the Dibrugarh veterinary department. Earlier counts include 70 at Dibrugarh University, 40 at Dibrugarh Airport, 15 at ICMR, 300 through adoption camps and rescue activities, and 970 in Dibrugarh town and market areas. Officials say sustained vaccination is a key public health tool to prevent rabies and will continue through coordinated drives with responsible care.

article.articleHeadline: New NGS facility at SGPGIMS to deliver faster, precise TB drug-resistance profiling
article.articleSummary: TB drug-resistance profiling in Uttar Pradesh could become faster and more accurate with SGPGIMS establishing the state's first Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) facility dedicated to tuberculosis. In Lucknow, Prof Richa Mishra notes the NGS unit is equipped with an Illumina MiSeq i100plus sequencing platform funded through CSR support from Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. SGPGIMS also conducted its first hands-on NGS workshop, 'From Sequence to Solution: NGS for precision TB Diagnostics.' The technology can potentially reduce the time to identify drug-resistance patterns from weeks to days, aiding clinicians in tailoring treatment. This development marks a significant advance for TB diagnosis and drug-resistance profiling in Uttar Pradesh, enabling more rapid, laboratory-confirmed insights to guide therapy.

article.articleHeadline: One baby orangutan develops fever at Odisha's Nandankanan Zoo, under observation
article.articleSummary: One of five baby orangutans quarantined at Odisha's Nandankanan Zoological Park since 8 September has developed fever, prompting ongoing veterinary observation as of 15 September 2026. The infant has had a high temperature since Sunday, with fever subsiding after medication but recurring, and remains stable under round-the-clock care. The other four infants are healthy and responding normally. Orangutans are not native to India. Experts say the fever's cause must be determined to assess risk to others; if infectious, it could spread to another infant; if non-infectious or stress-related, risk differs. Transport stress, possible low immunity, and colostrum history may contribute. Vets will monitor fever height, persistence, overall condition, and initial colostrum exposure. The five infants were rescued from a casuarina forest in Balasore district before arriving at the zoo.

Intravenous drug users account for about 65% of infections, driven largely by shared needle use; remaining cases are predominantly among sex workers, men who have sex with men, and transgender individuals. The report emphasizes ongoing transmission dynamics and the need for continued surveillance and access to treatment across Assam.

article.articleSummary: UNJA student team from Universitas Jambi has secured 2026 PKM-RE funding from Dirjen Dikti. The five-member, cross-disciplinary group—led by Muhammad Faris Rizqullah (Medicine, 2023) and including Nurul Fathiah Azzahra (Medicine, 2023), Anjeli Bismi Arsy (Biology, 2024), Kireina Nurfadhillah (Medicine, 2024), and Arum Kinasih Ramadhani (Pharmacy, 2024)—will develop Teh Niraga, a polyherbal tea from corn silk and red onion skin waste, combined with Phyllanthus niruri (meniran) and stevia. It targets antioxidant activity and dengue virus antiviral properties. In vitro assays and in silico simulations will assess molecular interactions with dengue proteins. The team aims to reduce dengue burden in Indonesia, including Jambi, and advance toward data generation for potential participation in PIMNAS in October 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Maternal and Infant Mortality Rates in Indonesia Are High, Health Minister Highlights Hospital Infection Cases
article.articleSummary: Infant mortality in Indonesia is about 30,000 per year and maternal mortality about 4,000 per year, according to Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin. Speaking Sept 14, 2026, to DPR Commission IX in Jakarta, he said Indonesia’s performance remains poor in ASEAN. West Java has among the highest rates, particularly in tertiary hospitals. He cited three districts/cities in West Java with elevated mortality and attributed several deaths to nosocomial infections from inadequate hospital sanitation and infection control. If death results from hemorrhage but occurs days after admission with infection, he said, infection management is at fault. The Ministry of Health will map high-mortality hospitals and provide direct mentoring. Patients will also input ratings and complaints, publicly displayed like e-commerce apps, to improve oversight—not as punishment but as constructive guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Yogyakarta strengthens TB prevention through ACF activities.
article.articleSummary: Yogyakarta City Health Office strengthens tuberculosis (TB) prevention and case finding through Active Case Finding (ACF) activities conducted July–August 2026, identifying 231 individuals as suspects who underwent further evaluation. Suspects with TB symptoms were asked to provide sputum samples for rapid molecular testing (TCM), followed by chest X-ray to assess lung status and detect possible TB among household contacts. If chest imaging is normal and no TB is diagnosed, eligible individuals may start tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT). If imaging shows abnormalities suggestive of TB, they receive treatment as TB patients rather than TPT. The effort aims to expand TPT coverage for household contacts of TB patients and to identify active cases in the community and at-risk groups. Preventive measures include clean-living behaviors, nutrition, physical activity, healthy housing, and BCG vaccination for children to reduce transmission.

article.articleHeadline: History of Pondok Gede Hajj Dormitory: Born from the Threat of the Eltor Cholera Outbreak.
article.articleSummary: El Tor cholera outbreak among Indonesian Haj pilgrims spurred the creation of Indonesia’s first Hajj Dormitory, Pondok Gede, in East Jakarta. Saudi medical checks found El Tor cholera among pilgrims from Sulawesi, prompting mandatory quarantine before entering the haram. In 1970, WHO designated Indonesia as affected by El Tor cholera, leading to a quarantine regime of five days before departure and five days after return (later shortened to three days pre- and post-travel in 1973). To avoid rising rental costs for temporary quarantine spaces amid shifting air travel, the government planned a permanent facility: SP-08/1974 established the Hajj Quarantine Dormitory Planning Team. About 15 hectares were allocated in Jalan Raya Pondok Gede, Pinang Ranti, Makasar, Jakarta Timur, in 1977; construction 1978–1979; officially opened in 1979. Governance moved from Proyek Asrama Haji to BPAH (1982), and since 2014 to UPT Asrama Haji Embarkasi Jakarta under the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah. Today the complex serves as a multifunction public space for education, worship, and UMKM.

Since 2024, the Health Ministry’s malaria-elimination roadmap targets 2,075,723 tests for Mimika by 2028, with elimination targeted by 2030. WHO estimates about 200,000 malaria cases in Mimika; with two million tests the yield would be ~200,000 positives. In 2025, 1.3 million tests identified 190,000 positives. article.articleHeadline: The Government Implements Several Preventive Measures to Anticipate Dengue Fever Outbreaks During El Niño.

Preventive actions focus on environmental cleanup to eliminate standing water, rapid early detection through blood tests, and recognizing dengue by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). He emphasized that Indonesian dengue mortality is currently well managed and stressed the need for fast detection. Despite the El Niño-related risk, there has not yet been a surge in dengue cases across Indonesia. The measures intend to strengthen surveillance and community cleanup to mitigate potential outbreaks during El Niño. Location: Jakarta, Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola outbreak in Kongo: Why it's so dangerous.
article.articleSummary: Ebola is spreading in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo as fast as ever, driven not by high transmissibility but by violence, displacement, weak authorities, and a dilapidated health system. The outbreak, first identified in April–May 2026 in the gold region around Mongbwalu, expanded through mobile populations and distrust of state institutions, hindering contact tracing across several provinces. The virus involved is Bundibugyo ebolavirus, which differs from prior Ebola strains, leaving uncertainty about how well existing vaccines and treatments work. Experts warn there is no miracle solution; success will hinge on trust, local collaboration, safe patient care, and persistent case finding and follow-up throughout the epidemic’s course.

Epidemiological tracing is complete; individuals not contacted by health authorities are not required to act. Laboratory testing is underway, with results expected in coming days. No confirmed Ebola case has been diagnosed in Israel to date. The World Health Organization notes the current Ebola outbreak has caused 3,269 deaths, predominantly in the Democratic Republic of Congo. This event underscores ongoing risk of imported Ebola cases and the need for rapid isolation, tracing and testing.

article.articleHeadline: Kinshasa: Physiotherapists Mobilized to Strengthen Poliomyelitis Surveillance - Le Potentiel
article.articleSummary: Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo — Physiotherapists, mobilized with WHO support, held a polio-awareness session at the Memling Hotel involving the Union des kinésithérapeutes du Congo to strengthen surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis (PFA). The initiative positions physiotherapists as critical in early alert, patient referral, and epidemiological surveillance, beyond rehabilitation, within polio eradication efforts. The event emphasizes integrating scientific knowledge with clinical practice to improve PFA surveillance, noting that sudden flaccid paralysis in a child is not automatically poliomyelitis and requires clinical and virological investigation. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative outlines four surveillance steps: search/notify PFA cases, transport stool specimens, identify poliovirus in the laboratory, and characterize/map viral strains. Polio is highly contagious via fecal-oral transmission; most infections are asymptomatic, but about 1 in 200 lead to paralysis, with 5–10% of paralytic cases resulting in death from respiratory failure. Case notification and lab confirmation drive eradication efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Ituri: Ebola response activities suspended in the zone.
article.articleSummary: Ebola response activities in the Damas health zone of Djugu district, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, have been suspended since Monday, September 13, 2026. All Ebola response operations are halted, including patient care, maintenance of treatment centers, contact tracing, dignified and safe burials, and prevention outreach. The strike follows a four-day earlier stoppage by drivers of response vehicles and ambulances over three months of unpaid allowances. Officials have not yet responded, and workers cite unfulfilled government promises to regularize their rights.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in eastern DRC: an unprecedented outbreak, an on-the-ground response.
article.articleSummary: Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo represents the largest outbreak the country has seen, driven by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus strain with no available vaccine or treatment. It spans five provinces—Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo—and from May 15 to July 31 recorded 3,674 confirmed cases and 1,621 deaths, with transmission outpacing response capacity. Memisa, a Belgian NGO, in collaboration with the Bunia Diocesan Office of Medical Works (BDOM Bunia), is supporting nine health zones by supplying hospitals and clinics with medical materials and medicines. Authorities emphasize rapid detection and community risk communication: adhere to hygiene, report suspected cases immediately, and avoid burying deaths without safeguards; protecting health workers remains challenging amid staff departures and reduced health-seeking behavior. In Bunia, a dedicated infectious-disease pavilion with isolation spaces aids the response. The piece links the surge to USAID funding cuts under Donald Trump, underscoring the need for resilient health systems.

article.articleHeadline: ZMB: Epidemic - 08-2026 - Anthrax (2026-09-14) - Zambia
article.articleSummary: Three suspected human anthrax cases were reported on 31 August 2026 from Kazembe and Kalimba in Mpika District, Muchinga Province, Zambia, amid reports of more than 90 animals dying of suspected anthrax in the Munyamazi River area and a hippopotamus carcass discovered. A Rapid Response Team employing a One Health approach—drawing on livestock, wildlife, clinical care, surveillance, and laboratory personnel—was activated to determine exposure sources and outbreak extent. Eight clinical specimens have been collected and sent to Lusaka for laboratory confirmation; none of the human cases required admission at this stage. Cases are clustered in specific villages and, in the current investigation, about 80% of suspected cases are male, with children aged 10–15 years accounting for roughly half. Consumption of meat from animals that died in the river area is a suspected exposure, with ongoing risk communication, surveillance, and coordination with animal health and wildlife authorities. No international assistance requested.

article.articleHeadline: Fever and vomiting in a 1-month-old baby; septic shock and multi-organ failure in critical condition.
article.articleSummary: On 14 September 2026, a 50‑day‑old infant from A Dơi commune, Quảng Trị Province, Vietnam, presented with fever, vomiting and frequent diarrhea, progressing to septic shock and multi‑organ failure due to a gastrointestinal infection. Dehydrated and in shock on transfer from Huong Hoa General Hospital to Quang Tri General Hospital, the child developed acute respiratory distress, liver and kidney dysfunction, electrolyte disturbances and coagulopathy. An urgent pediatric intensive care response included endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and early antibiotics, with 24/7 monitoring of vitals, urine output and labs. After aggressive resuscitation, infection was controlled and organ functions gradually recovered; vasopressors were tapered and the infant breathed spontaneously. After two weeks of treatment, the child was fully recovered with no sequelae and discharged. The report urges prompt medical evaluation for febrile, vomiting or diarrheal symptoms in infants under 3 months.

article.articleHeadline: Symposium highlights RSV risks in older adults
article.articleSummary: RSV poses a substantial burden for Vietnam’s ageing population, with modelling over five years projecting about 4.6 million RSV-associated acute respiratory infection cases among adults aged 60 and older, roughly 200,000 hospitalisations and about 18,000 deaths from RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease. At a symposium in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, experts urged proactive prevention for older adults and those with asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, diabetes or immunocompromising conditions. Vaccination is highlighted as a key protective measure, with vaccination counselling integrated into routine care across cardiology, respiratory, endocrinology, nephrology and geriatric services, and for discharge or transplant planning. International guidance from GOLD and CDC supports vaccinating high-risk groups. Policy context: Vietnam Ministry of Health Decision No. 1983/QD-BYT (July) promotes preventive vaccination, including RSV, influenza, pneumococcal, herpes zoster, hepatitis B and HPV. The event underscores the need for integrated prevention in aging Vietnam, with GSK Vietnam involvement.

article.articleHeadline: 5 Places in the Home That Should Be Cleaned Properly to Reduce the Risk of Disease Transmission.
article.articleSummary: As of 14 September 2026, seasonal temperature and humidity shifts raise susceptibility to respiratory infections such as influenza and RSV, along with bacterial diseases like pneumococcal infections and pertussis, and still-persistent measles, COVID-19, chickenpox, dengue, hand-foot-mouth disease, Japanese encephalitis, and meningococcal disease; with COVID-19 rising in some northern provinces. While season changes do not guarantee illness, risk increases with circulating agents, exposure, immunity, and environment. Emphasize cleaning high-touch surfaces: door handles, light switches; devices (TV remotes, smartphones, keyboards, mice); faucets and sink areas; dining tables and fridge handles; and bathroom fixtures, especially toilet flush levers, seats, door handles, and faucet handles. WHO and CDC advise cleaning (soap and water) first to remove debris, then disinfection if needed, focusing on surfaces used most. Do not mix cleaners; ensure ventilation; follow label directions; avoid unnecessary aerosol spraying. Hygiene, ventilation, masking when ill, vaccination remain essential.

article.articleHeadline: Artist Bao Bao in Critical Condition Due to Tuberculous Meningitis
article.articleSummary: Vietnamese artist Bao Bảo, 31, of the Huỳnh Long drama troupe, is in critical condition with tuberculous meningitis confirmed by CSF testing after fever, headache, and progressive neurological symptoms. He was hospitalized following fever and headache; on Sept 9 he developed facial droop and slurred speech, and by Sept 12 he was comatose, experiencing seizures and cyanosis, requiring sedation, intubation, and mechanical ventilation. He was transferred to another facility for continued treatment as of Sept 14, with his condition still critical and under intensive CNS infection management. Family and colleagues have urged support due to high treatment costs. Tuberculous meningitis is a severe extrapulmonary TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis affecting the meninges and spinal cord; initial symptoms are non-specific but can progress to headache, fever, neck stiffness, vomiting, altered consciousness, and seizures. The infection is airborne from pulmonary TB; meningitis itself is not directly contagious.

Industry leaders urge a ban on any meat products from ASF zones. Authorities explain that noodles with meat chunks or pork oil are not meat products yet heated products carry low risk, while raw meat and sausages remain highest risk and are forbidden for travelers and commercial imports. First-time penalties for travelers carrying ASF meat products are NT$200,000, with potential future tightening as of 2026-09-14.

article.articleHeadline: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 17 (31 August to 6 September 2026)
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease (BVD) outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is ongoing, with Situation Report No. 17 covering Aug 31–Sept 6, 2026. As of Sept 1, 2026, over 6,200 confirmed BVD cases and more than 3,000 deaths have been reported. Ituri and North Kivu remain heavily affected; ongoing transmission is reported in Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé near the CAR border, signaling cross-border risk to Uganda, Tanzania and other countries. The response includes mass health screenings (30,560,048 at points of entry/points of control), support to 230 PoEs/PoCs, and RCCE reach to 26,500,916 individuals. More than 50 IOM-managed IDP sites in Ituri and North Kivu are impacted by the outbreak amid WASH, health, and shelter vulnerabilities. 171 fatalities have been intercepted at PoCs. Preparedness and IPC, border surveillance, and pre-positioning are emphasized for cross-border protection, with Priority 1a (DRC, Uganda) and 1b (Burundi, Rwanda, South Sudan) and Priority 2 (Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, Zambia) in focus.

article.articleHeadline: Health advocates demand solutions to years-long TB drug shortage
article.articleSummary: TB drug shortages threaten treatment in the Philippines as of 14 September 2026, with first-line meds for drug-susceptible TB in short supply since late 2023 after DOH procurement failures. The country has the Southeast Asia region’s highest TB burden in recent years and, in 2024, the third‑highest global TB burden after Indonesia and India; TB treatment is free in government facilities via PhilHealth’s TB-DOTS package (over P7,000 total; reimbursements P12,000–P19,000). Health advocates urge the DOH to procure all first-line drugs, recalibrate distribution to prioritize local government units, and bolster PhilHealth reimbursements. Reports from TBPeople Philippines cite shortages in Manila’s Tondo, Rizal, Cavite, Bicol, Tacloban, Tawi-Tawi and Cotabato, with health centers hesitant to screen patients. KomuKonek data show 30 shortage reports across nine regions from 2025–Aug 2026. An Aug 25 urgent appeal called for improved procurement scheduling, preservation of the 2026 16‑million screening target, better regional reporting, stronger notification, expanded preventive treatment, and increased national-level procurement access to LGUs, noting bureaucracy as the root cause.

article.articleHeadline: What caused this woman's hallucinations? Doctors reveal an infestation of brain worms
article.articleSummary: Neurocysticercosis from Taenia solium eggs caused brain cysts in a 52-year-old woman in the Philippines, with four months of headaches and visual hallucinations and language disruption. Brain imaging showed cysts containing a scolex, diagnosing neurocysticercosis. The infection results from fecal-oral transmission: a tapeworm carrier sheds eggs in feces that contaminate food or surfaces. Exposure likely occurred in evacuation centers with poor sanitation. After antiparasitic treatment and seizure management, her symptoms resolved within a month as cysts shrank and the scolex disappeared on follow-up imaging. Neurocysticercosis can be fatal if inflammation and swelling occur or cysts obstruct fluid flow. The report notes other cases, including a Peruvian teenager with similar hallucinations and brain changes.

article.articleSummary: As of Aug 31–Sep 6, 2026, Hungary’s National Public Health Center released county-level infectious disease data, including Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén. No mass community gastroenteritis outbreak was reported. Pest County: 79-year-old man with suspected tetanus who received active vaccination after hospital admission. A 43-year-old man tested positive for dengue virus, infection acquired in the Philippines during the incubation period. Bács-Kiskun: a 6-year-old boy, vaccinated against the disease, suspected parotitis epidemica (mumps) with confirmatory tests ongoing; one imported viral hemorrhagic fever case reported this week. Budapest: an 83-year-old man with locally acquired West Nile fever; this year’s total West Nile cases is four, majority male (75%), mean age 68.3 years, all with neurological symptoms. Mpox: a 48-year-old man in Budapest and a 23-year-old man in Győr-Moson-Sopron; neither vaccinated. In Borsod, infections include campylobacteriosis (5), salmonella (5), rotavirus (2), viral hepatitis (18), and hepatitis A (17).

article.articleHeadline: Hospitals in Naga City at 'full capacity' with dengue patients
article.articleSummary: Dengue outbreaks in Naga City, Philippines, have surged to 495 confirmed cases with six fatalities as of 14 September 2026. City officials report about 300 dengue cases this month, prompting expanded hospital strain: three new wards at Naga City General Hospital opened on 11 September are already near full capacity, while the Bicol Medical Center – Department of Pediatrics has its ward at full capacity due to a sharp rise in pediatric admissions for dengue (and pneumonia). To manage confinement needs, the city government plans to add beds in hospital corridors. Naga City was placed under a state of calamity on 8 September because of the rising dengue numbers. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease, emphasizing urgent public health measures in the affected area.

article.articleHeadline: DOH logs 8,317 leptospirosis cases
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis in the Philippines rose to 8,317 cases from Jan 4–Sept 5, 2026, per the Department of Health, up 14% from 7,280 in 2025, with 457 fatalities (41% fewer than 2025). From Aug 9–22, 2,374 cases were recorded, a 332% jump from 550 (Jul 26–Aug 8). The National Capital Region leads with 3,191 cases, followed by Central Luzon (1,063), Calabarzon (831), Cagayan Valley (590), and Davao Region (404). Males account for 81% of cases; ages range from under 1 to 91. As of Aug 29, 6,253 cases had been recorded nationwide. Officials warn of a possible second wave about two weeks after mass flooding in Metro Manila and Central Luzon from monsoon rains. Transmission occurs via urine from infected animals (rats, pigs) or urine-contaminated floodwaters; symptoms include fever, vomiting, nausea, muscle pain, headache, and reddish eyes. Seek care promptly.

article.articleHeadline: Durandé uses a drone to map possible dengue hotspots in the Santa Edwiges neighborhood.
article.articleSummary: Drone mapping in Santa Edwiges, Durandé, Brazil, conducted by the municipal health surveillance team with Dangel, pilot for Tech Dengue, identifies potential dengue arbovirus hotspots to support vector control. The overflight targets areas that may promote Aedes aegypti proliferation, including rooftops with standing water, open water tanks, and pools. After the flight, coordinates and exact locations of identified points are handed to field inspectors to verify on site. The drone acts as a technical aid, enabling surveillance to reach sites difficult to assess from the streets and guiding preventive inspections. This activity, publicized by the Durandé City Hall, is part of ongoing dengue prevention and health surveillance strengthening, highlighting how technology aids early risk detection and targeted interventions to reduce arboviral transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Diagnosis of Yellow Fever puts the queen at death's door in The Nobility of Love - BH 24 Horas.

article.articleHeadline: Rocky Mountain spotted fever puts the North and Northwest of the state on alert | Bom Jesus | O Dia
article.articleSummary: As of 14 September 2026, two deaths from Rocky Mountain spotted fever (febre maculosa) have been confirmed in Rio de Janeiro's Northwest Fluminense and Norte regions: São Fidélis (death in August) and Bom Jesus do Itabapoana (death confirmed last week). The year’s first case occurred in early August. A joint task force mobilizes to curb the tick vector (carrapato-estrela), with field epidemiology, environmental surveillance, and population education. In Bom Jesus, targeted acaricide applications are underway, with field teams mapping likely infection sites and advising on domestic animal care and yard hygiene. In São Fidélis, riverbank and capybara (hosts) hotspots are restricted; the effort includes Defesa Civil, Meio Ambiente, Saúde, Emater, and hospital staff, who advise starting appropriate antibiotics before lab confirmation for suspected cases. Individuals with fever, severe headache, or rash after forest or river margin exposure should seek urgent medical care.

article.articleHeadline: The Ronaldo administration begins implementing the Wolbachia method to combat dengue, chikungunya, and Zika in Feira de Santana.
article.articleSummary: Feira de Santana, Bahia, Brazil began implementing the Wolbachia method on September 10, 2026, to curb transmission of dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. The program uses Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, reducing their ability to transmit the arboviruses. It is not genetic modification and seeks to establish Wolbachia in the local mosquito population for a sustainable effect. The rollout spans 12 months, starting with a three-month preparatory phase focusing on community engagement, space readiness, and staff training. Following preparation, Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes (wolbitos) will be released for six months in planned, monitored deployments. Monitoring relies on ovitrampas to assess Wolbachia establishment and guide surveillance and control efforts. The initiative is integrated with Inova Feira, applying artificial intelligence to automatically count mosquito eggs to enhance data analysis and surveillance.)

article.articleHeadline: Jacareí carries out a dengue control campaign; see neighborhoods and schedule.
article.articleSummary: Jacareí launches a dengue-control campaign to curb Aedes aegypti, the vector of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. The effort includes house-to-house visits, fogging, and the Cata-Treco junk-removal drive to eliminate water-holding debris. House visits target Jardim Primavera, Cidade Salvador, Bandeira Branca, Jardim Emília, and Novo Amanhecer. Cata-Treco runs Sept 15–18, covering multiple neighborhoods on each day (Tue: Jardim Pereira do Amparo, Jardim Mesquita, Jardim Esper, Terras de Santa Clara, Bandeira Branca I–II; Wed: Santa Maria, Prolongamento Santa Maria, Bandeira Branca I–II; Thu: Santa Maria, Prolongamento Santa Maria, Santana do Pedregulho; Fri: Igarapés, Bela Vista, 22 de Abril, Veraneio Ijal, Veraneio Irajá, Alvorada, 1º de Maio, Santa Paula, Rio Comprido). Residents must leave materials on the curb by 6:50 a.m. Nebulization targets locations with confirmed or suspected dengue cases, using insecticides approved as safe for people and animals. Dengue vaccination is available for ages 10–14 at 19 health units; four units offer extended hours (8:00–19:00) with tickets until 18:00: Santa Cruz dos Lázaros, Cidade Salvador, Parque Santo Antônio, Jardim das Indústrias.

article.articleHeadline: Health brings a dengue-control drive to Lealdade/Amizade and Vetorazzo.
article.articleSummary: Rio Preto's Health Department launches a new Saturday mutirão of health agents in Lealdade/Amizade and Vetorazzo to locate and eliminate Aedes aegypti breeding sites, the vector of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. The campaign, scheduled for Saturday, September 19, 2026, from 08:00 to 14:00, involves home visits and prevention guidance; residents should grant entry as teams are in uniform and badge-identified. To date, agents have inspected 43,637 properties on Saturdays. Additional actions during the week include Indoor Residual Spraying (BRI), nebulization, and maintenance of Larvicide Dissemination Stations (LDS). The municipality is deploying the Wolbachia method to reduce arbovirus transmission. The effort aligns with UN SDGs 3 (Health and Well-being), 16 (Peace/Institutions) and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals).

article.articleHeadline: Hospital treats 20 people after risk of contamination at a school in Rio de Janeiro | Rio de Janeiro | O Dia
article.articleSummary: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Twenty people (students and visitors) sought care at Hospital Municipal Lourenço Jorge for potential exposure to bloodborne infections after a science fair at Colégio Tamandaré in Recreio dos Bandeirantes from September 12–14, 2026. A student brought a glucose meter and a box of disposable lancets; one lancet was used on up to three individuals, sharing lancets created the risk. The activity was halted, equipment collected, and the responsible adult advised of the seriousness. The Municipal Health Secretariat instructed families to seek medical evaluation within 72 hours for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). On September 14, the Harvey Ribeiro de Souza Filho Municipal Health Center followed up with students who had not yet sought care. The 42nd Police Precinct (Recreio dos Bandeirantes) is investigating; no confirmed infections have been reported, only exposure risk.

article.articleHeadline: Iracemápolis Health Department begins Phase 2 of active case-finding campaign for tuberculosis | Rápido no Ar
article.articleSummary: Phase 2 of Iracemápolis, São Paulo, Brazil’s active tuberculosis (TB) case-finding campaign runs 16–30 September, Monday–Friday, 7:00–9:00 local time, at four health units (USF Dr. Angelo Arlindo Lobo, USF Angelina Platinetti Massari, USF Maria Neves Alexandrino, UBS Noé Franco de Campos). The effort, organized by the Municipal Health Department, aims to detect TB early, ensuring appropriate treatment and reducing transmission; sputum samples are processed within the local health network. This initiative seeks to improve cure chances through timely diagnosis in Iracemápolis. Translation note: disease is tuberculosis; location is Iracemápolis, Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Botucatu updates veterinarians on the current situation of sporotrichosis and leishmaniasis - Acontece Botucatu
article.articleSummary: On 14 September 2026, Botucatu's Zoonoses Control Unit (UCZ) held a meeting with veterinarians from public and private networks to discuss the epidemiological situation of sporotrichosis and leishmaniasis in the city. The UCZ team outlined the current epidemiological scenario for both diseases in Botucatu and detailed the main actions underway in the municipality. The program also provided guidelines and strategies related to rabies, a zoonosis requiring ongoing monitoring. Veterinarians play a critical role in identifying suspected cases, advising pet owners, and communicating with surveillance agencies. The collaboration seeks faster information flow and a stronger municipal response to zoonoses, aligning with a One Health approach that links human, animal, and environmental health.

article.articleHeadline: Amazonas strengthens the fight against malaria with the training of 15 indigenous spokespeople - MPPS.
article.articleSummary: Malaria diagnosis and certification training is underway in Amazonas, Venezuela, from September 14–23, 2026, at the Posada Manapiare in Puerto Ayacucho. Fifteen indigenous community spokespeople from difficult-to-access riverine municipalities are receiving technical tools to support local health work. Instructors Walter Camico, Karina Pacheco, and Thaidy Nieves cover malaria symptomatology, diagnostic methods, and treatment, with hands-on practice in preparing thick and thin blood smears stained with Giemsa, assessing sample quality, identifying Plasmodium species, and calculating parasitemia. The program strengthens the regional laboratory network and aims to credential participants to bolster prevention and epidemiological control of malaria in Amazonas. Supported by MinSalud and UNDP, the initiative emphasizes empowering indigenous communities to lead disease prevention as part of the national health strategy to advance eradication efforts in Guayana Venezolana.

article.articleHeadline: Thailand responds to reports of a COVID-19 outbreak: what's happening in Kazakhstan.
article.articleSummary: Thailand reports Phuket's COVID-19 incidence 514.85 per 100k as of Aug 31, ranking third nationwide behind Bangkok (643.65) and Chanthaburi (530.52). DCD attributes Phuket's island tourism and density to higher rates; officials call the situation seasonal with predominantly mild symptoms, not an outbreak. Omicron NB.1.8.1 remains dominant in Thailand, accounting for 524 cases (50.14%) since mid‑2025; no evidence of increased virulence. Globally, WHO data show continued circulation with low and stable positivity overall, but rates above 10% in Central America/Caribbean, SW Europe, and parts of Northern, Western, Southern, and Eastern Asia; a modest rise in a tropical South American country is noted. In Kazakhstan, 2026 has 87 confirmed cases with zero deaths; incidence down 3.7‑fold vs last year, averaging about 15 weekly. Omicron persists; weekly monitoring recommended; guidance emphasizes masks, ventilation, and seeking care if symptomatic.

article.articleHeadline: Thailand Responds to Reports of COVID-19 Outbreak: What is Happening in Kazakhstan
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 remains circulating globally but is not treating Thailand as an emergency. Phuket records a seasonal rise, with 514.85 cases per 100,000 as of Aug 31, ranking behind Bangkok (643.65) and Chonburi (530.52). The DDC notes most infections have mild symptoms and Phuket’s higher rate reflects dense tourism rather than a surge. The dominant Thai Omicron sub-variant is NB.1.8.1, with about 524 cases (50.14% of identified infections) since mid-2025, and no evidence of increased severity. Globally, SARS-CoV-2 continues with low overall test positivity, though rates exceed 10% in several regions; a slight uptick is seen in one tropical South American country. In Kazakhstan, 2026 totals reach 87 confirmed cases and zero deaths, about 15 weekly, with Omicron still circulating and ongoing weekly monitoring advised. Public-health guidance remains to avoid close contact, wash hands, ventilate rooms, and seek care if symptoms appear.

article.articleHeadline: Free rabies vaccination campaign targets 25,000 dogs and cats nationwide
article.articleSummary: Ghana's Veterinary Services Department launches a nationwide free rabies vaccination campaign targeting 25,000 dogs and cats in identified high-risk areas, running throughout September 2026. Aims to achieve zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030, aligning with World Rabies Month 2026 under the theme 'Stronger Together.' After the free vaccination period, pet owners will pay prescribed fees. The campaign emphasizes public education, reaching schools, religious institutions, and communities via traditional and social media, with educational materials in Twi, Ga, Ewe and Hausa. Pet owners are urged to ensure annual rabies vaccinations and to seek immediate medical attention after any animal bite or scratch, reporting the animal to the nearest veterinary centre. Rabies is virtually 100% fatal once symptoms develop, but preventable by vaccination. Non-vaccination may violate MMDA bye-laws. Support from MMDAs, civil society, religious/traditional authorities, development partners, and private sector is welcome for vaccines, logistics, and outreach.

article.articleHeadline: Ziro/Bakata: the army's agricultural volunteers launch an offensive against malaria vectors.
article.articleSummary: Malaria prevention efforts were stepped up in Bakata, Ziro Province, Burkina Faso, on 7 September 2026 as military agricultural volunteers (VDP) organized a sanitation day to curb mosquito breeding. Volunteers cleaned and weeded public spaces including the royal court, the Center for Health Promotion and Social Welfare (CSPS), and the communal VDP headquarters. Sita Kabré, head of the group, said the activity aims to improve living conditions and reduce larval habitats that support malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Residents were urged to join in maintaining their surroundings, especially by routinely cleaning compounds and public areas. The eco-citizens day, in the rainy season, seeks to lower malaria risk, reinforcing the ongoing public health concern of malaria in the region. Reported by Agence d'Information du Burkina (AIB).
